My guess is that NUnit has a dependency on Newtonsoft.Json v12. You can verify this by searching the `.deps.json` file generated in your test project's debug folder. Search it for all uses of `Newtonsoft`, and you should be able to see which referenced assemblies have dependencies on v12. To work around this error you'll need to add an explicit package reference to v13 in your unit test project or get rid of the reference that requires v12 if you can.

I use MSTest v2 instead of NUnit, and I have to deal with this because the `Microsoft.NET.Test.Sdk` and `MSTest.TestAdapter` packages depend on Newtonsoft.Json v10. So, I have to add an explicit package reference to v13 to force MSBuild to choose it as the primary version for my test project.

In case it helps, here's a relevant snippet from my UnitTests folder's Directory.Build.props file which pulls in these references:
``` XML
<ItemGroup>
	<PackageReference Include="Shouldly" PrivateAssets="all" />
	<PackageReference Include="Microsoft.NET.Test.Sdk" PrivateAssets="all" />
	<PackageReference Include="MSTest.TestAdapter" PrivateAssets="all" />
	<PackageReference Include="MSTest.TestFramework" PrivateAssets="all" />
	<PackageReference Include="coverlet.collector" PrivateAssets="all" />

	<!-- We have to include a primary reference to the version of Newtonsoft.Json we require since
	Microsoft.NET.Test.Sdk and MSTest.TestAdapter reference an older version of it (v10) per the
	generated *.Tests.deps.json files. If we don't include this reference, then we'll get MSBuild
	warnings where it chooses the older version as the primary reference.
	https://stackoverflow.com/a/24509329/1882616 -->
	<PackageReference Include="Newtonsoft.Json" PrivateAssets="all" />
</ItemGroup>
```

FWIW, I'm using [Central Package Management](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/nuget/consume-packages/Central-Package-Management), so my version numbers are factored out into a separate Directory.Packages.props file.

Also, it may be worth nothing for others that I only started running into this when I changed my `<PackageReference Include="Newtonsoft.Json" PrivateAssets="all" />` statements to include PrivateAssets="all". I'm transitioning to System.Text.Json instead, so I wanted my core libraries to stop advertising transitive dependencies on Newtonsoft.Json. That makes downstream projects have to explicitly reference Newtonsoft.Json if they still need it, which is good. But it exposed this MSBuild warning with unit tests due to MSTest's dependency on Newtonsoft.Json v10. When I wasn't using PrivateAssets="all", MSBuild silently picked v13 based on my core library's transitive dependency on that version, which trumped MSTest's v10 dependency.

Considering for how long the Newtonsoft.Json libarary is available and how widely Newtonsoft.Json is being adopted, a change in established default behavior of the library is astronomically unlikely.

The solution to the quagmire with recursive property behavior where the property returns an instance that is equal to the instance the property belongs to would probably be setting the Newtonsoft.Json setting `ReferenceLoopHandling` to `ReferenceLoopHandling.Ignore`.

If the recursive behavior is however an infinite/very deep nesting of unequal instances, then this setting might not help. In such a case, a custom ContractResolver that excludes specific properties from serialization would help (or, if the usage scenario is limited to a handful of types being serialized, perhaps custom JsonConverters might be an alternative).

(As a side note: Why this seemingly arbitrary condition on the observed problem being only related to unmanaged structs? I mean, if Vector3 were to have just an additional string field, it would not be an unmanaged struct anymore, yet the same problem behavior would still be observed. The problem of infinitely/very deeply nested property paths would in fact not only apply to value-type structs, but to reference types as well, if such a property would just be programmed in the "right" fashion...)

> (As a side note: Why this seemingly arbitrary condition on the observed problem being only related to unmanaged structs? I mean, if Vector3 were to have just an additional string field, it would not be an unmanaged struct anymore, yet the same problem behavior would still be observed. The problem of infinitely/very deeply nested property paths would in fact not only apply to value-type structs, but to reference types as well, if such a property would just be programmed in the "right" fashion...)

The idea being that an unmanaged struct is basically a binary serialization of itself already, serializing the entire thing would be no different than just copying the struct like you would normally do in C#. Where allowing object references opens you up to creating copies of objects that you don't necessarily want copied. The string case is less severe I suppose, but if you round trip a struct with a string the 2 string instances may not be ReferenceEqual.

I'd agree the change in default behavior could be an issue, but I could see this being a valuable setting at least. Serializing 3rd party types makes me want to eat buckshot for breakfast.

Well, it seems to me some piece of your code is manipulating the list while the serializer is serializing the list. Since List\<T\> is not thread-safe, this would be the precise outcome when one thread manipulates the list while another thread iterates over it. Solution to this problem is conceptually simple: Prevent the serialized list from being modified by some other thread while the serializer is processing it. How exactly this should be done depends on your actual code and the logic implemented by it, and i therefore would leave this to you to figure out as you are the one most knowledgable about your own code.

Yeah, you will have to pay attention to the default (de)serialization settings. Sometimes, Newtonsoft.Json's documentation doesn't make a good job of explaining things, which means sometimes you will have to scour it more thoroughly to find the pertinent information. Luckily, the documentation of the (de)serialization settings (and their default values/behaviors) is one of the first topics in its documentation and should be easily discoverable, i hope. And it's probably a good idea to read about _all_ those settings and their default values/behaviors, because the defaults can sometimes be different from what many would intuitively expect them to be.

If you look at the documentation for (de)serialization setting [`ObjectCreationHandling`](https://www.newtonsoft.com/json/help/html/SerializationSettings.htm#ObjectCreationHandling), you'll notice that its default value is _Auto_, which behaves as follows (excerpt from the documentation):
> **add** JSON values to existing collections during deserialization. 

So, in case of your List\<T\> example, it should now be clear how you end up with four elements: The two initial elements in the list plus the two elements from the json **added** during deserialization.

Another bit the documentation does not really clarify is that if the target collection is an array (which does not allow adding of elements) then Newtonsoft.Json will try to replace the existing array with a new array instance containing _only_ the deserialized collection elements but not containing the elements from the original array instance (permitting that the respective field/property can actually being set, or a parameterized constructor is being used during deserialization for passing the new array instance). 

Which all basically means, the observed default behavior can change depending on the concrete collection type vs. array at play here as well as whether it would be possible for the deserializer to pass a new array instance into the target field/property/constructor.

The problem is actually in the declaration of the `TestClass`. Nothing in that class ensures that the _Child_ member is **not** null when the _TestClass.TestProp_ get accessor is being invoked.

Newtonsoft.Json does not define in which particular order properties of an object are being deserialized, and thus you cannot rely on any particular order of members being populated/assigned in the target object. It is not a bug in Newtonsoft.Json if some code path of some Newtonsoft.Json class tries to access the `TestClass.TestProp` property, and then the `TestClass.TestProp` getter tries to access another member that is _null_. That the `It_should_serialize_prop_with_custom_getset_no_settings` test case is working is just lucky circumstances.

Who knows what other (de)serialization settings, JsonConverters and/or (custom) ContractResolvers, or perhaps even a future Newtonsoft.Json version might exhibit a similar deserialization behavior as your failing test case using StringEnumConverter. Instead of relying on poorly defined or outright undefined details of the deserialization behavior it is in my opinion a better approach to write the _TestClass_ more robustly so that none of its code attempts to dereference possible null references...

comments.body:
System.ExecutionEngineException indicates that some internal state inside the CLR / runtime went horribly wrong.

In all likelihood this is _not_ caused by Newtonsoft.Json.

The method call on which this exception is thrown (regardless of the method call being a method from Newtonsoft.Json or some other method) is typically _not_ the cause of the problem (the method call basically just being the event that makes the CLR detect the invalid internal CLR state, but didn't cause that invalid internal CLR state). The exeption occuring is often just a symptom of a problem occuring earlier in the program execution. The causing problem might even have been occuring _substantially_ earlier before that exeception has been thrown.

This makes System.ExecutionEngineException one of the hardest and nastiest exceptions to troubleshoot. There is no way around, you will have to diagnose this problem yourself, and quite likely this will be a rather tedious and frustrating endeavour, unfortunately. :-(

Some of the typically culprits that can produce such a problem:

- unsafe code twiddling with pointers in a way that corrupts memory (managed heap, memory internal to CLR, etc...), especially - but not limited to - pointer arithmethic that blindly and incorrectly assumes the program is running as 32-bit process while it actually runs as 64-bit process (or vice versa)
- invoking native code with incorrect values or that is buggy which can lead to it accessing and modifying memory it should not (and thus potentially corrupting the managed heap or CLR-internal memory states)
- COM interop going wrong
- IL code generators emitting incorrect IL code
- corrupted assemblies (whether they are part of your program of part of the .NET installation)
- defective/glitchy RAM modules (or any other related hardware part of the computer's memory subsystem)

You are deserializing a `JsonPatchDocument<TModel>`. You are **not** deserializing a _MyPatchModel_.

I have to admit having a hard time wrapping my head around what you are trying to achieve. Logically, the declared type of a property should have no bearing on the which object a reference refers to. The unambiguity of a reference should normally not rely on arbitrary meta-information external to the json data itself. Nor should the semantics of a reference normally change based on the declared property type (i.e., the same reference should still refer to the same object regardless of the property this object is being assigned to is declared as `IShape` or `Rectangle`, for example.)

Which leads me to the question (my apologies for my response essentially not being more than just some question being thrown back at you): Why would you need the type of some property to resolve references? (Asked differently: why exactly would your reference resolver have to rely on that _AssetsSystem.GetAsset_ method?) Or is the object referred to not an actual part of the json data being deserialized?

This is in Unity and I am trying to store references made to Unity assets, so objects outside of the JSON data being serialized. I am trying to avoid assigning unique GUID string ids to each asset, and instead keep it readable.
My solution instead of the above was to include the type information in the string reference - so something like 'Sword-InventoryItem', then when parsed it checks 'InventoryItem' assets for that 'Sword' name.
My thought was definitely this shouldn't be needed though if I could just have the context give me some information on what's being deserialized. Especially when dealing with back compatibility as types / names of assets change.

Will _all_ the asset json objects in your json data ever be such references, or do you have deal with a mix of asset objects in the json data that are either fully serialized objects or asset references?

In case of the asset objects in the json exclusively being string references, could you perhaps switch to a JsonConverter instead (while restricting this converter to your asset type(s))?

And making _LastAssetTypeDeserializing_ a [`ThreadLocal<Type>`](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.threadlocal-1) should allow you to run deserialization jobs concurrently (or [`AsyncLocal<Type>`](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.asynclocal-1), although Newtonsoft.Json's deserialization routine is not async).

_UPDATE:_ While it is not a bug in the library itself, there is arguably an issue with the documentation at https://www.newtonsoft.com/json/help/html/M_Newtonsoft_Json_JsonConvert_DeserializeXmlNode_3.htm. It is written in a way that can lead users to false expectations of what the _encodeSpecialCharacters_ parameter is apparently supposed to do vs. what it it is actually unable to do.

------- 

Not a bug.

The problem lies in your chosen element name. The `$` character is **NOT** allowed for XML element names (See XML spec about element names here: https://www.w3.org/TR/xml/#sec-starttags).

Even if you don't care about the XML spec, `System.Xml.XmlDocument` (that's what you are trying to derserialize your json into here) won't tolerate `$` in element names (proof here: https://dotnetfiddle.net/XN8QY7). So, in conclusion, Newtonsoft.Json can't really help you bending _System.Xml.XmlDocument_ to your will.

I strongly suggest to adhere to the XML specification and avoid `$` characters in element names. If you can't, you will have to find another way to convert your json into a spec-violating XML document, unfortunately, and then you will also have to make sure that whatever will consume such an invalid XML document can actually handle such violations of the XML spec.

I know this character is not allowed, and unfortunately I cannot work around the fact that it appears in the JSON I am trying to deserialize.
In the definition of the method `DeserializeXmlNode(string value, string? deserializeRootElementName, bool writeArrayAttribute, bool encodeSpecialCharacters)`, the following is written for `encodeSpecialCharacters`.

> A value to indicate whether to encode special characters when converting JSON to XML. If true, special characters like ':', '@', '?', '#' and '$' in JSON property names aren't used to specify XML namespaces, attributes or processing directives.Instead special characters are encoded and written as part of the XML element name.

To me it does not seem far-fetched to think that setting `encodeSpecialCharacters` to false would not encode the `$` since it is mentionned in the description. I hope this is not a fallacy.
I guess the real fix would be to rework this description.

> I know this character is not allowed, and unfortunately I cannot work around the fact that it appears in the JSON I am trying to deserialize. Unfortunately, this means in consequence you can forget about using _XmlDocument_[^1] or _XElement_, because neither will allow `$` characters in element names. That also means that you can forget about Newtonsoft.Json's _built-in_ Json-to-XML conversion, as the only conversion targets offered are either _XmlDocument_ or _XElement_. Depending on what you want to achieve, i would either suggest to first look for an alternate XML processor that's tolerant with regard to XML spec violations and then evaluate whether and how Newtonsoft.Json could be utilized to feed/deserialize the json data into that XML processor. Or, if the usage scenario is simple enough to only require XML text to be produced, you could perhaps deserialize the json data as a JObject/JArray/JValue representation and then "manually" generate the XML text from it (thus bypassing _XmlDocument_ and _XElement_). > I guess the real fix would be to rework this description. I fully agree with you on this point. The doc should -- needs to -- be more precise, and not only in this particular place. [^1]: Just a wild idea -- although personally, i would rather try finding an alternative XML processor before following this wild idea: It might (or might not; i haven't tried) be possible to sub-class the _XmlElement_ and possibly the _XmlDocument_ class in way allowing to bypass element name validation, thus possibly allowing you to use the _XmlDocument_ infrastructure in your code. I am basing this idea purely on related properties and methods in _XmlElement_ / _XmlDocument_ being overridable (i also haven't checked whether there are functional dependencies on internal/private methods that can't be called from a sub class; trickery with reflection not withstanding). I can't tell if this idea would practically work and not just result in a finicky and unreliable house of cards, though...

Unfortunately, the only way to "tell" Newtonsoft.Json to use such sub classes of _XmlElement_ / _XmlDocument_ (assuming this wild idea would actually work), would be in duplicating the code of the [XmlNodeConverter](https://github.com/JamesNK/Newtonsoft.Json/blob/master/Src/Newtonsoft.Json/Converters/XmlNodeConverter.cs), changing it to use your _XmlElement_ / _XmlDocument_ sub-classes as well as disabling the bit that encodes invalid characters. This modified converter could then be used in a call to `JsonConvert.DeserializeObject(json, new ModifiedXmlNodeConverter())` or something...

It might be better to give up on the idea of creating wrong XML texts just for the sake of keeping dollar signs.
Thank you very much for your time.

Come to think of it, your problem is neither with MissingMemberHandling nor with the get-only property. If i am not mistaken, to create Exception instances, Newtonsoft.Json _has_ to use the [Exceptions streaming contructor](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.exception.-ctor?view=net-6.0#system-exception-ctor(system-runtime-serialization-serializationinfo-system-runtime-serialization-streamingcontext)). However, this requires the SerializationInfo instance passed to this constructor to be fully populated, including property members that have default values. But, if you take a look at your serialized json for the exception, note that all properties with default values are missing. For reference, that are the json properties an Exception instance serialized by Newtonsoft.Json instance will have including properties with default value: ``` "ClassName": "System.Exception", "Message": "some message", "Data": null, "InnerException": null, "HelpURL": null, "StackTraceString": null, "RemoteStackTraceString": null, "RemoteStackIndex": 0, "ExceptionMethod": null, "HResult": -2146233088, "Source": null, "WatsonBuckets": null ``` (Dotnetfiddle: https://dotnetfiddle.net/Ap8FH7) You will notice that there are some properties missing in your json. But you can't fix this with Newtonsoft.Json's MissingMemberHandling, because the requirement for certain properties being present in the SerializationInfo instance is hard-wired in Exception's streaming constructor due to it using the _SerializationInfo.GetString / GetValue / GetInt32_ methods (which will throw if the property is not in the SerializationInfo instance). To know precisely which properties are required to be present in the SerializationInfo and therefore in the json data, look at the source code of the streaming constructor: https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/3ff8d262e504d03977edeb67da2b83d01c9ed2db/src/libraries/System.Private.CoreLib/src/System/Exception.cs#L40-L52; With respect to the RestoreRemoteStackTrace method called by the constructor, see here: https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/blob/3ff8d262e504d03977edeb67da2b83d01c9ed2db/src/coreclr/System.Private.CoreLib/src/System/Exception.CoreCLR.cs#L16-L43). Any property that is obtained from the SerializationInfo **not** using a _Get***NoThrow**(...)_ method is required to be present.
In conclusion, to solve your problem i would suggest to configure the serializer producing the json to include all exception properties even if they contain default values, and deserialization should then succeed without requiring further intervention. But if you are unable to change the configuration of the serializer producing the json, then use a custom JsonConverter for creating the Exception instance (for example by letting the custom JsonConverter deserialize any Exception json data first as a JObject, then add any missing required properties to the JObject and its descendent JObjects, and finally deserialize the JObject into an Exception the custom JsonConverter will return.) Perhaps there are good examples of such a custom JsonConverter to be found on stackoverflow.com, but i haven't looked and i will leave searching for suitable candidates to you...

Unfortunately i can't really help you with your problem; aside from suggesting you check every assembly/dependency your software is using  -- including each dependency's dependencies -- whether some have dependencies on Newtonsoft.Json of a different version than your project is using.

But i want to point out that "Runtime version" in your secreenshot refers to the version of the CLR (the Common Language Runtime) required to execute the IL code in the assembly. Do **NOT** mistake it as Framework version.

All the .NET Framework 4.x versions (including .NET Framework 4.5) use the CLR v4.0. Thus, naturally the Newtonsoft.Json library version for .NET framework 4.5 would list runtime version 4.0.x (again, runtime version does _not_ equate framework version).

 (In comparison, the older .NET framework 3.5 uses CLR v2.0. And fortunately, starting with .NET 5, there is no separate runtime (CLR) version anymore that could differ from the .NET version, so such confusions will be a thing of the past...)

In my opinion this is leasing msbuild giving error on build. The strange thing is that if the assembly is directly referenced by a .net 4.0 library it would compile. I don't have any experience with Assembly Explorer (it's a feature of jetbrain's Resharper, right?).

But note that both the error and what you see in Assembly Explorer are consistent. Both strongly indicate that there is actually no Newtonsoft.Json assembly for .NET Framework 4.0 present during your build process, but in actuality Newtonsoft.Json assembly for .NET Framework 4.5 is present. The error [MSB3275](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/visualstudio/msbuild/errors/msb3275?view=vs-2022) indicates that a dependency could not be resolved because the dependency was for a framework version higher than the depending library or the softare project build target allows. (English error message quoted from the MSB3275 documentation i linked to: "_The primary reference 'reference' could not be resolved because it has an indirect dependency on the assembly 'assembly-name' which was built against the 'version' framework. This is a higher version than the currently targeted framework 'version'._")

I also took a look into the nuget package for Newtonsoft.Json 13.0.1 and the config/spec files and assemblies contained therein, and i did not find anything suspicious there.

Thus, based on the given information i tend to disagree with your statement that

> [...] the version above is the .NET Framework 4.0 version of Newtonsoft library, it shouldn't display targeting 4.5 (as displayed in the upper part of the screenshot).

Given that both the error message and Assembly Explorer agree on the Framework version, i rather tend to believe the display of Assembly Explorer is truthful, and that the version above is indeed the .NET Framework 4.5 version of Newtonsoft library, not the .NET Framework 4.0 version as you seem to think.

I do not share your suspicion that the Newtonsoft.Json 13.0.1 assembly .NET Framework 4.0 or its manifest is somehow borked. Based on the (somewhat limited) information in your report, me looking into the nuget package, and a lack of other people reporting issues similar to what you seem to suspect, i don't think that this case is likely. I am not saying that this is impossible; but i am saying that all i know about your issue is implying a different probable cause.

Personally, my suspicion is strongly aimed at your project and/or build process _somehow_ pulling in the actual Newtonsoft.Json 13.0.1 assembly for .NET Framework 4.5 instead of the intended/desired variant for .NET Framework 4.0.

Double check that your project files use the package reference for the [official Newtonsoft.Json nuget package](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Newtonsoft.Json/#package-reference) or a direct reference to the correct Newtonsoft.Json assembly DLL, and are not by chance referring to an unofficial Newtonsoft.Json package or assembly that has been modified by a 3rd party. Also make sure that the nuget.org feed is being used to fetch the Newtonsoft.Json nuget package.

Is the local nuget cache perhaps at fault? If the problem is not with your build configuration/process somehow referring directly or indirectly to the incorrect Newtonsoft.Json assembly variant (which i still do not rule out; i don't know enough of your project and build setup to discard this possibility outright), perhaps  the local nuget cache got corrupted somehow? (This could possibly also explain why a simple switch to Newtonsoft.Json 12.0.0 allowed for a successful build.)

If you are willing and able to try, try removing Newtonsoft.Json version 13.0.1 from the nuget caches used by your build servers (so that the nuget package will have to be fetched again), then clean and rebuild your project/solution, and see whether it rectifies the situation. Alternatively, to verify that the local nuget cache is not corrupted, you could also manually download the nuget package (https://www.nuget.org/packages/Newtonsoft.Json/13.0.1), extract it (for example with 7zip; nuget package files are essentially ZIP archives) and do a binary comparison of the files in the local nuget cache and the respective files from the manually downloaded nuget package.

I'd suggest closing this issue and asking it on stackoverflow.com - its not at this point proven that the issue is something that's specific to this library

(edited to add: I have nothing to add regarding your response - you may well be right, but for me the fact remains that way more people will look and think about this on SO)

I see. It did work around my problem.

But do you really think the original code should break? Nothing obvious should alert you that stack overflow can happen (it didn't even ask for circular check) + even if you specify no circular check is needed (`ReferenceLoopHandling.Serialize`), it still won't work.

> But do you really think the original code should break?

Absolutely yes. Because of how you implemented the Equals method -- _you_ (not the library!) essentially programmed infinite recursion here (well, technically the library of course contributes to the problem, but you coded against documented -- albeit rather _poorly_ documented -- behavior of the library). It is not the job of the library to work around your particular Equals implementation, it's _your_ job to use the library accordingly based on its documented behavior and functionalities.

_BUT_: I am actually not really blaming you for being frustrated and expecting the library to _just work_. I totally agree with that.

If there is any blame to put, it is neither on you nor on the library itself -- but squarely on the library's documentation. 

Although the documentation is [explaining the use of Equals and the default ReferenceLoopHandling mode being Error](https://www.newtonsoft.com/json/help/html/SerializationSettings.htm#ReferenceLoopHandling) (with the Error mode obviously requiring "reference" checks to be able to detect circular "references"), it could make a _much much_ better job in explaining the library's "out of the box" default behavior. A user of the library will be unaware of this unless they specifically look for this (which they won't when they are unaware of it) or come across it by chance when perusing the documentation (and then would still demand of the reader to make the context switch from "references" as in ".NET object references" to the different meaning in how Newtonsoft.Json uses the term "references", otherwise the reader can quickly get confused by the documentation).

Running into a problem with the library like yours should ideally be answerable with "RTFM", but regrettably, Newtonsoft.Json's documentation is not one of its strengths, in my opinion :-( (I do love the library due to its versatility. But my love of the library does not extend to its documentation, as you might be able to tell...)

I'm just frustrated that 1) `JsonConvert.SerializeObject()` will call `Equals()` and 2) `ReferenceLoopHandling.Serialize` still does partly relies reference loops, which it defiftely can skip even for performance gain. Both are quite unintuitive...

_(My apologies. I deleted my previous comment, as it was wrong due to me not realizing that the issue manifests specifically only with the 0x85 control character in your XML data.)_

> What we see is the encoding is not maintained and some new character has been replaced in original characters.

Incorrect. Take a hex editor and look into your XML file. You will find those control characters already in the XML file (specifically, their respective UTF-8 code sequences. For the 0x85 control char, the UTF-8 code sequence would be 0xC2,0x85). There are no new or changed characters in your Json output. It's just that the control character 0x85 (which is already in your XML file) is being represented in the json by the escape sequence `\^E` (which is a valid json character escape sequence).

It seems that is/was an intentional design decision by the author of Newtonsoft.Json to escape the control character 0x85 in the generated json text for some reason:

https://github.com/JamesNK/Newtonsoft.Json/blob/52190a3a3de6ef9a556583cbcb2381073e7197bc/Src/Newtonsoft.Json/Utilities/JavaScriptUtils.cs#L209-L217

But i don't know why this decision was made. The JSON spec itself does not demand the escaping of the control characters 0x85, 0x2028 and 0x2029.

Unfortunately, this behavior is hard-coded and cannot be configured. Thus, if you can't live with \\uXXXX escape sequences in your json, i guess the easiest workaround is to do a `string.Replace("\\^E", "\^E")` on the json string returned by _JsonConvert.SerializeXmlNode_. (Although, normally it shouldn't matter whether the character appears literally or as numeric escape sequence in the json data. The Json spec explicitly allows for any characters to be represented by `\uXXXX` escape sequences.)

----------------------
Side note: Your XML contains quite a few control characters like 0x81 and 0x85. Are they an intentional part of your XML file, or are they just there by accident? To me, their presence does not look intentional, and i suspect this to be an unintentional by-product of some dirty or buggy text processing used during handling (creation, transport, storage) of the source data that is being put into the XML. If they are not an intentional part of the XML data, perhaps take a look at how these XML files are being generated and whether something could be done to produce clean XML without those control characters.

comments.body:
Well, [Unix Epoch time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unix_time) is traditionally given in seconds. And that's what _UnixDateTimeConverter_ does: treating numbers as Unix Epoch time given in _seconds_. However, here you got a _millisecond_ timestamp. The exception is just the side effect of the number being treated and added as seconds to Unix epoch, and thus exceeding DateTime.MaxValue. Unfortunately, _UnixDateTimeConverter_ can't be configured to accept millisecond timestamp values. To support millisecond timestamps, i would suggest writing your own converter. The implementation should be rather simple and straightforward (you could use UnixDateTimeConverter's source code as a template for your own implementation).
That _UnixDateTimeConverter_ just throws the _ArgumentOutOfRangeException_ without providing useful information about which part of the Json input caused the issue is still something that needs improvement in my opinion.

comments.body:
Your problem is not caused by Newtonsoft.Json, but rather by your own code.
(Please close this issue report here, as the issue is not with Newtonsoft.Json.)

If you set a breakpoint on the DailyTask constructor (which Newtonsoft.Json obviously has to call to create a DailyTask instance) and single-step through this constructor, you'll notice that `DailyTask.GetNextDue()` is getting stuck in an infinite loop.

Why does `DailyTask.GetNextDue()` get stuck? Look at the `while` loop:
```VB
_NextDue = OriginalDue
While DateTime.Now > _NextDue OrElse _Weekdays.GetValue(_NextDue.DayOfWeek) = 0
    _NextDue = DateAdd(DateInterval.Day, 1, _OriginalDue)
End While
```
 The exit condition of this `while` loop depends on the value of `_NextDue`. The value of `_NextDue` is first initialized as the value of `OriginalDue`, but after that it will always be `DateAdd(DateInterval.Day, 1, _OriginalDue)`.

Note that the value of `_OriginalDue` is not changing during the execution of the `while` loop. So, with respect and within the scope of to the `while` loop, you can see `DateAdd(DateInterval.Day, 1, _OriginalDue)` as an unchanging, quasi-constant value (and therefore you can also consider `_NextDue` be an unchanging, quasi-constant value once `DateAdd(DateInterval.Day, 1, _OriginalDue)` has been assigned to it.)

Thus, if neither the value of `OriginalDue` nor the value of `DateAdd(DateInterval.Day, 1, _OriginalDue)` are satisfying the exit conditions of the `while` loop, your program will be forever stuck in this `while` loop.


I guess the `while` loop should be rather:
```VB
While DateTime.Now > _NextDue OrElse _Weekdays.GetValue(_NextDue.DayOfWeek) = 0
    _NextDue = DateAdd(DateInterval.Day, 1, _NextDue)
End While
```
(i.e., the next value of `_NextDue` should not be the next day after `_OriginalDue`, but the next day after the current `_NextDue`)

I am not in any way associated with the Newtonsoft.Json project, but here is my 2c worth of opinion:

There is a huge elephant in the room with asking to change the default behavior of the library. Newtonsoft.Json is one of the most popular (if not the _most_ popular) json library for .NET, with an extremely wide adoption both in open/libre as well as commercial software since a very long time already. As such, changing the default behavior of the library, no matter how good the argument for doing so, incurs a huge risk of breaking compatibility and potentially introducing subtle bugs with those existing software projects and deployments. With libraries that popular and wide-spread, it is a very good strategy to be extremely conservative and defensive against changing established behaviors or APIs. Since the solution is relatively cheap and simple by instructing Newtonsoft.Json to read floating-point numbers as `decimal`, i don't see compelling reasons so far that would justify taking the risk involved in breaking with long established default behavior (even if that default behavior happens to really suck sometimes...). The Newtonsoft.Json library comes in variants for .NET Standard 2.0, the older .NET Famework 2, .NET Famework  3.5, .NET Famework 4, .NET Famework 4.5, and for some other framework targets.

The library trying to use `System.Security.Permissions` is an indication that you use the Newtonsoft.Json library variant for .NET Framework 4.5 or older. Which is not the correct variant if your project targets .NET Core or .NET 5.

To fix your problem, make sure your project is using the Newtonsoft.Json library variant for **.NET Standard 2.0**.

comments.body:
This is not a bug. The true/false values in Json are lower-case. In other words, capitalized False or True do not represent boolean values in json.

Quoted from the the Json spec (http://www.ecma-international.org/publications/files/ECMA-ST/ECMA-404.pdf):

>These are the three literal name tokens: 
> true U+0074 U+0072 U+0075 U+0065 
> false U+0066 U+0061 U+006C U+0073 U+0065 
> null U+006E U+0075 U+006C U+006C

Note that the Json spec goes to even specify the ordinal character value of each of the characters in those value literals. A boolean false value in json must therefore be represented by all-lowercase `false` according to the json spec.

Having capitalized literals `True` or `False` in a json document violates the Json specification, thus technically such a json document isn't actually a proper json document to begin with.

I suggest to focus your engery on trying to convince the developer responsible for the producer of such invalid json documents to fix whatever it is that produces such broken json. If that is not feasible, i am afraid you will have to manually replace all those illegal value literals in the json string/document yourself (for example, by utilizing some regex replacement or some such), before feeding the repaired json document to the deserializer.

comments.body:
Well, you are both wrong and yet kinda right.

The wrong bit first: _JObject_ itself possesses no _Merge_ method. Therefore, The JObject.Merge contract cannot be wrong, as there is no JObject.Merge to begin with.

The _Merge_ method is from _JContainer_, the base class for _JObject_ (both the [JObject documentation](https://www.newtonsoft.com/json/help/html/Methods_T_Newtonsoft_Json_Linq_JObject.htm) as well as Intellisense will tell you that). _JContainer_ is also the base class for _JArray_ -- and this is important to understand why the parameter type of the _Merge_ method is not _JObject_. Because _JArray_ accepts enumerables (with elements that are either JValue, JObject, JArray) for merging.

Still, in my personal opinion, your post has merit and has a point. Because it underscores the _Merge_ method being a poorly designed API that invites misunderstandings and confusion, and also highlights the lack of documentation surrounding this method. In my two-cents-worth-of opinion, a much better API design would have been to let JObject and JArray implement their own  distinct _Merge_ methods with matching parameter types respectively, either hiding/shadowing the underlying base _JContainer.Merge_ method or getting rid of _JContainer.Merge_ altogether (although the latter might break code that specifically calls _Merge_ on JContainer references...). But i fear it's a case of _what's done is done_, unfortunately :-(

var receiptValue = json.SelectTokens("$.franchiseSale.sale.items[*].totalValue").Values<decimal>().Sum();

More information: this problem exists in version 12.0.3. If you set MaxDepth to a value known to the "The reader's MaxDepth of XX has been exceeded" exception, it results in the same stack overflow exception killing the IIS process. Therefore, the "FIX" for vulnerability https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-5crp-9r3c-p9vr in 13.0.1 by changing the MaxDepth default to 64 is insufficient, because it still results in the IIS process terminating when exceeded.

After spending more time debugging the code of Newtonsoft.Json, I've found the cause of the problem. In IIS, the default stack size for a thread is 256KB:
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/troubleshoot/developer/webapps/iis/site-behavior-performance/default-maximum-stack-size-thread

When a json file with a depth of 64 is parsed, and an exception occurs at this level (any exception, MaxDepth exceeded, Unexpected character encountered, etc), the exception is thrown, caught and rethrown repeatedly as the stack unwinds. This process of catching and rethrowing the exception numerous times ends up causing a StackOverflowException IF the code is running in a thread provided by IIS (w3wp). The same json file parses fine in a console application, because the default stack size is 1MB.

Since the type of exception does not matter, this really has nothing to do with MaxDepth setting, other than it was the error that originally manifested the problem. To prove this, I crafted a json file that contained unexpected characters for a property value at depth 67. I set MaxDepth to a value higher than the max depth in the json file. Parsing this file results in an Unexpected character exception from Json.Net, and when the exception is thrown, caught, and rethrown repeatedly as the stack unwinds, a StackOverflowException results, crashing IIS.

Another piece of data: If I set MaxDepth to 32, and parse a json file that is deeper than this, the MaxDepth exceeded exception is indeed thrown, but the process of propagating the exception as the stack unwinds does not result in a StackOverflowException.

Now we know the cause, the question remains what to do about it. 64 is not a safe value for the default MaxDepth setting when running in IIS. But, a malicious json file with bad characters at this depth can bring down IIS if the MaxDepth is set to some other high value.

This looks strange. The information in your issue report does not give a hint aside from a supposed mismatch between the Json data structure and the C# object graph you try to deserialize into as indicated by the exception.

Can you provide a self-contained code example that reproduces the problem and can be simply copy-pasted into dotnetfiddle or a console project in VS? Because, I did a quick'n'dirty code test on dotnetfiddle (https://dotnetfiddle.net/vPOP2r), and i cannot reproduce...

Alright. I know _what_ causes the problem, but i do not really know _why_... (as of now). Your `TrainingExercise` class has a constructor with an `int sets` argument. Changing the name of this constructor argument (for example to `int numberOfSets`) will solve the issue. Changing the name "Sets" of the public field to something else will not solve the issue, however. (In your report you mentioned the field variable "Sets" which i assumed you were referring to the field name "Sets" itself not the constructor argument name. But maybe i was misunderstanding your explanation there...) This is how i imagine the problem manifests: As Newtonsoft.Json has to create _TrainingExercise_ instances, it has to invoke the constructor with values for each constructor argument. It tries to do so by mapping each constructor argument with the value of a Json property (of the respective Json object) with a (case-insensitive) matching name. According to the constructor argument "sets", Newtonsoft.Json looks in the _TrainingExercise_ Json object for an the "Sets" property, and finds it. And then proceeds to attempting to read/parse an integer value, but finds a Json array instead.
_EDIT: Ignore the paragraphs below. There is a rather easy answer to my confusion, given in my follow-up comment below :-)_ But there is a "But". I big one... I said "_this is how imagine_" with a reason. Which totally confuses me, and which is also why i wrote in the beginning that i don't know why it happens. When reading your report, i already had a hunch it might be the constructor argument `int sets`. That's why i included a constructor with a `int sets` argument in my dotnetfiddle as well. But my dotnetfiddle does not fail, which is why i discarded my hunch. And this is also why i do not entirely trust my imagination here. I still have no clue of _why_ your code is throwing when the argument name in the _TrainingExercise_ constructor is `int sets` whereas my dotnetfiddle is not throwing. Hmm, puzzling... perhaps it might require a certain depth of nested Json objects to be triggered, perhaps it might be something else. As of now i have no solid idea, though...

Update to my last post: I am a dumbo. It's obvious why my dotnetfiddle does not throw despite the constructor argument.

In my original dotnetfiddle, my code itself creates the JsonModel instance and passes it to the JsonConvert.PopulateObject method, thus Newtonsoft.Json won't create another one (and thus does not invoke the constructor, obviously.). If i alter my dotnetfiddle so that Newtonsoft.Json actually has to create a _JsonModel_ instance, then my dotnetfiddle throws in the same manner as your code: https://dotnetfiddle.net/cGlouL

I am an idiot :-)

@elgonzo Yeah I also had thought about the conflict between the "int sets" in the constructor and my List Sets... but I always thought it would be case sensitive and constructor variables would be ignored. (But I do not know because Iam new to the newtonsoft library). Changing the name of the List Sets only helps if you delete the old Json before executing the code and create a new one with the new list name.

But my question is now: Is it correct that it throws an exception or is it not? Because I would not expect this behavior because of a constructur parameter.

comments.body:
Not really a bug...

There is no json array to be considered. The `]` is a red herring. There is a value there that is a valid string according to JSON syntax rules. And that string value `"SomeUnion"` is what `JToken.ReadFrom` reads, hence no error. (Btw, there is no specific _JValue.ReadFrom_ implementation; the compiler will simply resolve _JValue.ReadFrom_ to _JToken.ReadFrom_).

That _JToken.ReadFrom_ should attempt reading an JSON array when confronted with your "json" string is a misplaced expectation. It reads whatever token (or JSON data type, if you will) it detects, which in this case is just the JSON string `"SomeUnion"`, and it doesn't care whatever else follows after that token. In this sense, `"SomeUnion","foo"]"` would be no different than for example `"SomeUnion"this is totally not json anymore...` whether there is some bracket in the "tail" after `"SomeUnion"` or not.

If you expect your JSON data to be an array, you can attempt to load it as a _JArray_ by using the [JArray.Load method](https://www.newtonsoft.com/json/help/html/M_Newtonsoft_Json_Linq_JArray_Load.htm), like:
```C#
var res = JArray.Load(reader);
```
This will then also throw an exception if no valid JSON array can be obtained from the reader.
If using a _JsonReader_ is not a strict requirement, you could alternatively also use the [JToken.Parse(string) method](https://www.newtonsoft.com/json/help/html/Overload_Newtonsoft_Json_Linq_JToken_Parse.htm), which consumes the entire json string and not just whatever starting portion forming a valid JSON data type like _JToken.ReadFrom_ does.

If all you want is to see whether there is additional text following after the read json value, you could also just call `reader.Read()` after calling _JToken.ReadFrom_.

comments.body:
This is an effect of current msbuild versions producing portable PDBs by default. Portable PDB's are identifiable by a "BSJB" signature at the beginning of the PDB file.

Old versions of the build tools (including Microsoft.Build.Tasks) don't have support for portable PDBs. Older frameworks (specifically .NET framework 4.7 and older) only support the older type of PDB files that are identifiable by a "Microsoft C/C++ MSF 7.00" signature at the beginning of the PDB file. Only starting with .NET framework 4.7.1 portable PDBs are supported properly. See also this discussion: https://github.com/dotnet/sdk/issues/1238

The author of Newtonsoft.Json could change the project file to let it produce the old type of PDBs for framework targets older than 4.7.1 by setting _DebugType_ to _Full_ or _PdbOnly_  for those framework versions, like:
```
<DebugType Condition="'$(TargetFramework.TrimEnd(`0123456789`))' == 'net'">Full</DebugType>
```
(This is from the top of my head and unverified.)

The condition i have chosen relies on the fact that Newtonsoft.Json does not have targets for .NET framworks 4.7.x nor 4.8, thus it is sufficient to just test for the pattern "net<Number>" to identify framework targets without portable PDB support.

That's the behavior as mandated by Newtonsoft.Json's default DateTime format string - it only writes out fractions of a second if they are non-zero.

If you want to change how DateTime's are being formatted during serialization, you can specify your own DateTime format string through the `JsonSerializerSettings.DateFormatString` property. Documentation at https://www.newtonsoft.com/json/help/html/P_Newtonsoft_Json_JsonSerializerSettings_DateFormatString.htm. Btw, in this documentation page, note the default format string using the "[FFF...](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/base-types/custom-date-and-time-format-strings#uppercase-seconds-f-fraction-specifier)" format specifier for the fractions of a second, mandating the observed behavior.

Thanks. I can confirm that setting the `DateFormatString` as follows:

```
            var settings = new JsonSerializerSettings
            {
                DateFormatString = "yyyy-MM-ddTHH:mm:ss.fffffffK"
            };
```
produces a uniform JSON output

```
DateTime.UtcNow:The JSON representation of  21/08/2021 15:41:12 is                                  "2021-08-21T15:41:12.9201873Z"
DateTimeKind.Utc without milliseconds specified:The JSON representation of  25/12/2020 23:59:55 is  "2020-12-25T23:59:55.0000000Z"
DateTimeKind.Utc with milliseconds specified:The JSON representation of  25/12/2020 23:59:55 is     "2020-12-25T23:59:55.1230000Z"

```

I was aware about the `DateFormatString` setting parameter. However, I had not paid attention to the capital "F" in the default settings - which only takes into account the most significant digits of the seconds fraction.

Would be nice to know what was the rationale for choosing `yyyy-MM-ddTHH:mm:ss.fffffffK` over the more consistent `yyyy'-'MM'-'dd'T'HH':'mm':'ss.FFFFFFFK` ?



Thank you.

When serializing/storing/logging DateTime's, in most scenarios fractions of a second don't matter (i.e., are assumed to be zero). Think of any given time of day -- outside of highly specific scenarios (such as where precise sub-second timestamping is required) the resolution of time of day is normally only given as hours : minutes : seconds.

Thus, it makes sense from a general point of view that when a DateTime does not carry fractions of a second those fractional non-significant zeroes won't be included in the formatted DateTime string.

If you just add a reference to your library DLL in your WpfApp4 project, Visual Studio will **NOT** automatically try resolving the dependencies of that library DLL. Thus, Visual Studio will not copy the Newtonsoft.Json DLL into your build output directory. This would also happen with any other DLL your ClassLibrary1 depends on and which is neither a framework DLL nor part of the WpfApp4 references.

Either also add the Newtonsoft.Json DLL itself to your WpfApp4 project, or add ClassLibrary1 as a project reference (this requires the ClassLibrary1 project to be in the same solution, as you have donw with WpfApp1 (for project references, Visual Studio recognizes the dependecies of that other project based on the information it finds in that project's .csproj/.vbproj file).

(By the way, you looking at other nuget packages is a red herring. The nuget package manager itself resolves assembly dependencies for nuget packages being installed based on information in the respective nuget packages. Based on that, the nuget package manager will not only add the library from a nuget package to your project, but also add the other libraries the nuget package library is depending on to the project. Problems like these are not caused by _JsonConvert.SerializeObject_, and are normally caused by one of three things:

1. The serialized json text itself is intact and accurate (using UTF-8 encoding), but a wrong text encoding is used when reading/inspecting the json text back.

2. The string produced by _JsonConvert.SerializeObject_ is transmitted by some code/library which does not enforce UTF-8 encoding on the receiver/reader side. (That includes code/libraries that transmit strings using UTF-8, but using a protocol not supporting UTF-8 or failing to signal the correct encoding to the receiver.)

3. The original text values got already mangled before being fed into the json serializer. This can happen if there are some faulty text processing/conversion steps before serialization happening (Like for example, if the text is being passed between different tools/libraries each doing their own text encoding handling. This would also include some unusual faulty custom JsonConverter mangling data. )

I can't tell which of the three problems are happening in your situation, because the perceived (reported) outcome of those problems can be indistinguishable from each other. The basic issue here is as follows. 

The JSON standard is a textual (Unicode) standard.  In JSON numbers are untyped (beyond being distinguishable as numbers).   They are simply represented as some sequence of Unicode decimal characters unlimited in magnitude or precision.

But BSON is a binary standard in which numbers are typed, and of some fixed size and precision.  You can see the specification here: https://bsonspec.org/spec.html.  The relevant binary "Basic Types" are:

<!--StartFragment-->

byte | 1 byte (8-bits)
-- | --
int32 | 4 bytes (32-bit signed integer, two's complement)
int64 | 8 bytes (64-bit signed integer, two's complement)
uint64 | 8 bytes (64-bit unsigned integer)
double | 8 bytes (64-bit IEEE 754-2008 binary floating point)
**decimal128** | **16 bytes (128-bit IEEE 754-2008 decimal floating point)**

<!--EndFragment-->

And are represented as follows:

<html><body>
<!--StartFragment-->

element | ::= | "\x01" e_name double | 64-bit binary floating point
-- | -- | -- | --
  | \| | "\x02" e_name string | UTF-8 string
  | \| | "\x03" e_name document | Embedded document
  | \| | "\x04" e_name document | Array
  | \| | "\x05" e_name binary | Binary data
  | \| | "\x06" e_name | Undefined (value) — Deprecated
  | \| | "\x07" e_name (byte*12) | ObjectId
  | \| | "\x08" e_name "\x00" | Boolean "false"
  | \| | "\x08" e_name "\x01" | Boolean "true"
  | \| | "\x09" e_name int64 | UTC datetime
  | \| | "\x0A" e_name | Null value
  | \| | "\x0B" e_name cstring cstring | Regular expression - The first cstring is the  regex pattern, the second is the regex options string. Options are  identified by characters, which must be stored in alphabetical order.  Valid options are 'i' for case insensitive matching, 'm' for multiline  matching, 'x' for verbose mode, 'l' to make \w, \W, etc. locale  dependent, 's' for dotall mode ('.' matches everything), and 'u' to make  \w, \W, etc. match unicode.
  | \| | "\x0C" e_name string (byte*12) | DBPointer — Deprecated
  | \| | "\x0D" e_name string | JavaScript code
  | \| | "\x0E" e_name string | Symbol. — Deprecated
  | \| | "\x0F" e_name code_w_s | JavaScript code w/ scope — Deprecated
  | \| | "\x10" e_name int32 | 32-bit integer
  | \| | "\x11" e_name uint64 | Timestamp
  | \| | "\x12" e_name int64 | 64-bit integer
  | \| | **"\x13" e_name decimal128** | **[128-bit decimal floating point](https://github.com/mongodb/specifications/blob/master/source/bson-decimal128/decimal128.rst)**
  | \| | "\xFF" e_name | Min key
  | \| | "\x7F" e_name | Max key

<!--EndFragment-->
</body>
</html>

As you can see, the BSON spec distinguishes between an 8-byte double and a 16-byte decimal.  So it would be quite reasonable to expect that `BsonDataWriter` would write a `decimal` to a `decimal128`.  Unfortunately, it seems this is not implemented.  [`decimal128`](https://github.com/mongodb/specifications/blob/master/source/bson-decimal128/decimal128.rst) was introduced in MongoDB 3.4 in 2016-06-06 but Newtonsoft's BSON support was introduced in version [3.5.6](https://github.com/JamesNK/Newtonsoft.Json/releases/tag/3.5.6) in 2014 which predates `decimal128` -- and it seems that `BsonDataReader` and `BsonDataWriter` have not been updated to support this type.  There is not even a value (of 19) corresponding to `decimal128` in [`BsonType`](https://github.com/JamesNK/Newtonsoft.Json.Bson/blob/a1db92678e7e72eb733f37079f3a93bfb6215338/Src/Newtonsoft.Json.Bson/BsonType.cs) at the moment.

So, a reasonable request would be to support reading and writing of `decimal128` as well as automatic serialization of .NET `decimal` from and to this format, possibly with some configuration option to preserve the current behavior.

But since the BSON format itself is fixed precision, using `FloatParseHandling` to determine whether or not to read an 8-byte BSON double as .NET decimal or double doesn't really make sense.

Ah here we go.  This looks to duplicate [Support for decimal #7](https://github.com/JamesNK/Newtonsoft.Json.Bson/issues/7) over at [`Newtonsoft.Json.Bson`](https://github.com/JamesNK/Newtonsoft.Json.Bson/issues):

> The BSON specification at (http://bsonspec.org/spec.html) has a datatype for decimal. The current implementation does not properly support this. The BsonWriter will write a decimal value as a BsonType.Number which is a double and therefore my decimal precision is lost.
> 
> I tried subclassing the BsonWriter, but it doesn't look like I can extend the classes to add this support.
> Are there plans to support the decimal datatype?
> Any other way I can use bson and work with decimals?

Any fix for this ?

Why do you have defined the same json property name for both `A.Id` and `B.Id`? Both have an `[JsonProperty("id")]` attribute. That's the crux of the problem.

What's the point of having the same json property name for two different properties (which we have here; just in case you are unaware: note that `B.Id` is hiding `A.Id`. `B.Id` is **not** overriding `A.Id`). Trying to include both properties with the same json property name in the serialization will lead to a json object with duplicate property names (which will probably be a problem -- or at least a headache -- when trying to consume/deserialize such json data). If only one of `A.Id` or `B.Id` should be serialized, one of the two `[JsonProperty("id")]` is unnecessary and should be replaced by `[JsonIgnore]`, solving your problem.

@elgonzo I need both properties as B would be the model that I will be deserializing an HTTP response too and A would be the normalized model between all HTTP responses I receive. Therefore I need both JsonProperty attributes as one will be to deserialize and the other to serialize. Due to the nature of how horrible data is sent, this is our only approach. However, your response prior to the edit did the trick! So thanks a lot.

My apologies for deleting my original post, which i deleted when i suddenly noticed that there are two "id" json properties and i went like "wait a minute... does that really make sense?" Still, i am glad you saw it and it helped you before i deleted it. Now i wish i could bring my original post back, but it seems to be gone for good. :(

(By the way, my explanation about the contract resolver was not correct. `A.Id` will be part of the properties collection for type `B`. It's just that the duplicate json property name then leads to the exclusion of `A.Id` further down the line...)

Your code does not demonstrate the issue you describe. It seems to work as intended as far as i can tell. Look at the array definition in the XML sample you have given. It defines `ARRAY [0..1, 0..3] OF INT`. This translates to a two-dimensional array with the the respective dimensional lengths of 2 and 4. The json produced by your code contains the array `[[0,0,0,0],[0,0,0,0]]`, which is basically a table with two rows with 4 elements/numbers each, matching the definition as given by the XML.
But i guess i know what the problem is: It looks like you got confused by how the debugger presents the data in your screenshot (and so did i when i looked at the screenshot and the coloring). In your debugger screenshot, note the green number tuples in the first upper red rectangle. Those numbers themselves are **not** the array content of the `MyItemVariableTCP.Value` property. Rather, those `(0, 0)`, `(0, 1)`, ... , `(1, 2)` are the row/column coordinates of the respective array cells in your two-dimensional cells (the values of those cells being 0 are shown on the right hand of your screenshot). The value of each individual array cell is presented here by its "coordinate" in the two-dimensional array. If you plot these coordinates out, you'll realize that you have a two-dimensional array in `MyItemVariableTCP.Value`, with two rows (the row coordinate) and 3 elements per row (the column coordinate). This corresponds perfectly with the json you get. Also, in the debugger screenshot in the lower red rectangle, note that the `Value` array is shown as a whole (unlike the display in the upper red rectangle, the individual array element are not displayed in separate lines), also showing two rows with 3 elements each. I have annotated your screenshot to make this clearer: ![Untitled](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/6129198/121569100-b935b100-ca20-11eb-9e5b-853d0c64a5ab.png) That said, i have no idea how the final part of your issue report (the lines about `Dim MyTableau (1,1)` and so on) relate to your code or your screenshots...

Thank you for your reply,
I now understand the difference between the interpretations of the array value displays for vb and json.
The only problem is while deserializing, as my Value property is an object (contains different types of values), i was thinking of directly fetching this object as a Vb array. Here is my confusion.
So I will have to rebuild the array by interpreting the value of the property after deserialization.
[0,0,0], [0,0,0] will give an array (1,2) with (0,0) = 0, (0,1) = 0 ... etc
[1,2,0,0], [10,0,0,0] will give an array (1,3) with (0,0) = 1, (0,1) = 2 .... (1,0) = 10 ...etc

Is there another way to reconstruct the arrays?

Since the `Value` property in your model class is type `object`, Json.NET has no idea about the intended data type during deserialization and thus deserializes the value of this property as one of the concrete `JToken` types (`JValue`, `JObject`, `JArray` depending on what the actual content of the respective json property is).

Unless you allow Json.NET to store type information along-side the serialized `Value` property data,  you have to do the multi-dimension array conversion kinda manually, unfortunately. You didn't say how exactly you reconstruct the n-dimensional array. In case you are not aware of this already, you could create a type object for your n-dimensional array (using `Type.MakeArrayType(int dimensions)`) and then using JToken's/JArray's `.ToObject(Type t)` method with the type object created to create the array in at once. Something like (sorry, C# again. I am not really a VB programmer):

```c#
if (DeserializedItemVariableTCP.Value is JArray ja)
{
    var dimensions = ... Inspect the JArray ja to get the number of dimensions
    var multiDimArrayType = DeserializedItemVariableTCP.TypeVariable.MakeArrayType(dimensions);
    var array = ja.ToObject(multiDimArrayType);
    ...  array is ready to be used ...
}
```


On the other hand, if it would be permissible for you to let Json.NET store type information in the json -- that is not your custom type information, but type information Json.NET and other serializers understand -- you could probably avoid this manual processing of the `Value` property after/during deserialization by simply annotating the `Value` property with the JsonPropertyAttribute and setting its TypeNameHandling parameter accordingly (https://www.newtonsoft.com/json/help/html/P_Newtonsoft_Json_JsonPropertyAttribute_TypeNameHandling.htm), something like this:

```
Public Class ItemVariableTCP
    ....
    <Newtonsoft.Json.JsonProperty(TypeNameHandling:=Newtonsoft.Json.TypeNameHandling.All)>
    Public Property Value As Object
    ....
End Class
```

Hello,
I used the type name handling used when serializing the Value property as described in your comment.
(<Newtonsoft.Json.JsonProperty(TypeNameHandling:=Newtonsoft.Json.TypeNameHandling.All)>)

It works perfectly without intervention on the reconstruction of the array. It is much simpler.

Many thanks for your follow-up.

You misunderstand. StreamingContext.Context is not used nor created by the serializer.

Providing a StreamingContext.Context is up to you, the user. It always has been (even in the original context of using .NET's own Binaray

Create a `StreamingContext` instance (no, not just only StreamingContext.Context, but rather the complete StreamingContext) with whatever StreamingContext.Context you like and assign it to the [JsonSerializerSettings.Context](https://www.newtonsoft.com/json/help/html/P_Newtonsoft_Json_JsonSerializerSettings_Context.htm) property. This StreamingContext should then be passed to your serialization callbacks.

Hum, I see, I missed that property in JsonSerializerSettings... Thanks for pointing out. In fact, that creates a nice (but still solvable) chicken-egg problem since we need to pass the JsonSerializer in the StreamingContext which is passed to JsonSerializerSettings to create the JsonSerializer we need to begin with...

But still that leaves no option to review/manipulate the Json from the callback or am I missing some else ?

Hence maintaining this ticket as an improvement suggestion for the team to review.

What is the purpose of manipulating the json? I can't help but feel that this is some kind of XY problem that might be solved more elegantly in a different manner instead, but since i don't know any details about your circumstances my hunch might very well be wrong...

Thanks for offer, we solve it differently. But I still have the feeling there are some huge room for improvements with the callbacks to support more scenarios. It might possibly require adding some extended method signatures with more parameters for smooth/transparent transitions.

To give you a bit of the context where we found the actual limitations with callbacks (I am fully aware we can do it using  ContractSerializer instead). Some lib actually expects the class name as the root json property name. We initially attempted to solve it through callbacks and extended property. Hence the need to pass/retrieve the current SerializerSettings down the tree.

Accessing the raw json is not useful for that scenario but I strongly believe a general purpose library should eventually offer this possibility as well. I have not estimated the effort vs benefit of this feature here. If effort is indeed quite low, I might as well bring my own contribution.

You can actually control the json output to a high degree,by directly writing to the JsonWriter. It would also be possible to mix such "manual" writing to the JsonWriter with the serialization process where the serializer still writes the bulk of the json output (as i will demonstrate in a small example code i linked below).

From the little i know about your situation, your problem seems to be solvable relatively comfortably with a (small-ish?) custom JsonConverter that will be used by the serializer. This converter basically has to do the following:

- The converter has to restrict itself to your model types, but not handle any other types.
- In case your model classes use attribute annotations or ShouldSerialize* methods to determine whether a property should be serialized or not, get the json object contract for the type of the object to be serialized from which to get the list of properties that are allowed to be serialized (otherwise just use reflection to acquire and iterate over all properties).
- Iterate over the properties and check the type of the values in them, and partially manually write out the json object.  If the type is one of your model types, write the type name json property name (otherwise, do as you need/want; like for example writing the "normal" property name or something). Then let the property value being serialized by the serializer.

See here a quick'n'dirty example: https://dotnetfiddle.net/xsQNXk

Some notes about my example:
- Look at the `RootModel.SingleNestedModel` and `NestedModel.Child` properties and how their name changes to the type of the object assigned to it (which can be different from the property type itself) in the json result.
- Note that the properties that are not of my example model types (such as the string/int properties, and the enumeration-like array property) maintain their property names in the json output.
- Also note that my little example converter does not ignore default values except _null_ (such as the `0` value in the `Value` property, for example).
- With such a converter, the json will be written like that "directly" without requiring manipulation of the json "after the fact".

You will certainly need to adapt it to achive the desired application-specific behavior (i doubt there is a general-purpose behavior that would be satisfiying, as questions around how to deal with properties having null values assigned and what about two or more different properties having object instances of the same type assigned, leading to duplicate json property names, etc... depend largely on application-specific rules and constraints).

If you need a behavior that substantially differs from model class to model class, you might relocate the json writing logic of the converter into an instance method of your model classes, and change the converter so it only forwards the call to WriteJson to the respective method of the model object instance.

comments.body:
You have a number of ways to achieve this. I normally prefer one of these two approaches if i want opt-in behavior and/or conditionally select the properties for (de)serialization:

1. Choose an opt-in model where every property participating in (de)serialization has to be explicitly annotated by an attribute. You can use either attributes provided by Newtonsoft.Json's (see the fist code example here: https://www.newtonsoft.com/json/help/html/SerializationAttributes.htm; note the OptIn parameter on the [JsonObject] attribute). Or, alternatively you can use .NET's own `[DataContract]`/`[DataMember]` attributes if you want to don't want to make your data models dependent on Newtonsoft.Json.

2. Write a custom contract resolver that for (a) given type(s) collects the properties that should participate in (de)serialization. A simple example of that is the code example titled "Conditional properties with IContractResolver" you can find here: https://www.newtonsoft.com/json/help/html/ContractResolver.htm. The obvious difference to that simple example, in your case the condition is not the name of the property but the class in which a property has been declared (i.e. [MemberInfo.DeclaringType](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.reflection.memberinfo.declaringtype?view=net-5.0#System_Reflection_MemberInfo_DeclaringType)). And don't forget to set your custom contract resolver in your JsonSerializerSettings (see the very first code example on the page illustrating how to configure the JsonSerializerSettings with a contract resolver)

There are a few other avenues like even more other attributes or serialization callbacks, but i leave it to you to peruse the Newtonsoft.Json documentation. If one of the two ways i mentioned above is not to your liking, i would recommend looking at Newtonsoft.Json's [serialization attributes guide](https://www.newtonsoft.com/json/help/html/SerializationAttributes.htm) and [serialization callbacks guide](https://www.newtonsoft.com/json/help/html/SerializationCallbacks.htm).

Thanks, the option 2 I think I had implemented: [Json.NET.FlexibleContractResolver](https://github.com/GF-Huang/Json.NET.FlexibleContractResolver). But I think this is still not convenient and concise enough.

If it is not flexible enough and the attribute-based approach is impractical for you, write your own contract resolver. I am unable to suggest more because all i know about your circumstances is basically the little you have written in the title of your topic, and i don't have the faintest idea what you would consider being convenient and concise with regard to your problem :(

Yeah, this unfortunately does not work directly. The ShouldSerialize* method is a companion method to the property and would have to be declared with the property together in the same type/class.

If you want/need to stick with the ShouldSerialize* approach, you could write a custom contract resolver that is working around this issue by using reflection to collect the properties and trying to find matching ShouldSerialize* methods regardless of where they are declared in the inheritance chain. (But then again, since this would require a custom contract resolver to make it work, you could just simply write the contract resolver without relying on ShouldSerialize* methods, if preferred...)

(This will convert the parsed string back into a json representation, including any json-specific escape sequences for non-printable control characters and other characters with special meaning in json. Note that it is not guaranteed to yield a result identical to the source json string in any case; for example, the json string `"H\u0065llo"` will be parsed as the string `Hello`, and converting it back to json you will still get `"Hello"` instead of the `"H\u0065llo"` as in the source json.

comments.body:
> why are the values trimmed?

Because `JToken.Parse` / `JObject.Parse` uses an internal `JsonTextReader` for parsing the json text which operates in `FloatParseHandling.Double` mode by default. And you are not able to change the mode of this internal JsonTextReader from the "outside", unfortunately. :-(

However, there are alternatively ways to read Newtonsoft.Json.Linq jtoken types with `Decimal` for floating point numbers, until this limitation is (hopefully) being eliminated.

One such way is leveraging the `JToken.Load` method, which accepts a `JsonReader`. Thus, FloatParseHandling mode of this JsonReader can be set to Decimal accordingly like:
```
string jsonText = ...
using var jsonRdr = new JsonTextReader(newStringReader(jsonText)) { FloatParseHandling = FloatParseHandling.Decimal };
var jtoken = JToken.Load(jsonRdr);
```

Another way would be using `JsonConvert.Serialize` instead of `JToken.Parse`, with the FloatParseHandling mode of the default serialization settings set to Decimal:

```
JsonConvert.DefaultSettings =
    ( ) => new JsonSerializerSettings
    {
        FloatParseHandling = FloatParseHandling.Decimal
    };

string jsonText = ....
var jtoken = JsonConvert.DeserializeObject<JToken>(jsonText);
```
Note that it in this particular case it is sufficient to specifiy `JToken` as the deseralization target type. The correct matching concrete Newtonsoft.Json.Linq instance type (like `JValue`, `JObject`, `JArray`) will be created depending on the json text,

Dotnetfiddle demonstrating both approaches: https://dotnetfiddle.net/sn42pr
thanks a lot

It has to use opt-in for [DataContract]/[DataMember], because that is the specified and documented behavior for these attributes ([relevant doc for \[DataContract\]](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.runtime.serialization.datacontractattribute#remarks), [relevant doc for \[DataMember\]](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.runtime.serialization.datamemberattribute#remarks)).
