I ve got this issue on 12.0.3 nuget version.
Runtimes 3.1.100 and 5.0.100

This is not a bug in Json.NET, but a bug in your project.

Before i explain what happens on a technical level in your code there, i want to point out a major flaw in your ISomeJsonConverter: From what i can tell, the ISomeJsonConverter should be invoked when serializing an ISome instance. But all the converter does is calling the serializer again to serialize the object. There is no point in doing that. The JsonConverter attribute tells the serializer to not serialize an ISome instance the normal way as the serializer would do, but rather invoke the ISomeJsonConverter. But then, all the ISomeJsonConverter is to tell the serializer to serialize the ISome object instance the normal way anyway. If the converter just invokes the serializer with the given ISome object instance again, what is the point of having that converter?

But back to why your serialization code loops in one case, but not in the other...

In the first case - the JsonConverter attribute associated with the ISome interface itself. the serializer eventually has to serialize an object instance that implements ISome. So, it invokes the ISomeJsonConverter associated with this interface type. The ISomeJsonConverter just tells the serializer to serialize the object that implements ISome. So the serializer invokes the ISomeJsonConverter associated with this interface type. The ISomeJsonConverter then tells the serializer to serialize the object that implements ISome. So the serializer invokes the ISomeJsonConverter ... add nauseum... there is your loop. Because every time the serialize has to serialize an ISome instance, it sees and obeys the JsonConverter attribute associated with the type.

Removing the JsonConverter attribute from the interface type will break this loop. But then, why does the loop not happen if you have the JsonConverter attribute on the Other.SomeImpl property?

In the second case (JsonConverter attribute only on the Other.SomeImpl property), the serializer will eventually serialize the SomeImpl property of the Other object instance. Without looking at the type of the object assigned to the property, the serializer invokes the ISomeJsonConverter with the property value (an object implementing the ISome interface). The ISomeJsonConverter tells the serializer to serialize this object implementing the ISome interface. Note that the ISome interface itself, nor any member of the ISome interface is associated with the ISomeJsonConverter. Thus, when serializing the object implementing ISome, the serializer won't ever come across a JsonConverter attribute attached to the ISome interface or its members, so there is no situation that the converter will be called recursively when serializing the object implementing the ISome interface.


Lastly, an advice: stackoverflow.com is a much better place for asking questions about how to correctly use Json.NET. Not only will your question/problem be seen by many, many more eyes than here on the issue tracker, but you would probably also get an answer much, much quicker than here - if you are getting an answer here at all (keep in mind, this issue tracker here is for reporting and following up on bugs in Newtonsoft Json.NET itself, not about bugs/issues with code that merely uses this library incorrectly, so problems with user code might perhaps not get much attention here). Newtonsoft Json.Net's homepage also encourages people to ask on stackoverflow.com if they struggle with how to use Json.NET correctly...

JArray is derived from IEnumerable<JToken>.

The JToken enumeration of an JArray are the elements in the array. Query the [Type property](https://www.newtonsoft.com/json/help/html/P_Newtonsoft_Json_Linq_JToken_Type.htm) of every element JToken to see whether it is a value or an object.

Whether you use a loop or some Linq construct is up to you, but no matter what you have to enumerate the whole array to see whether it consists of objects only or values only, or something else. (If you like it risky and want to play fast&loose, you might choose to check only the type of the first element and then blindly assume all other elements in the array are of the same type...)

The answer given is technically not correct. Json.NET does not require you to make the class or properties public.

Yes, making the type and property accessors public is one way to address the problem. But there are different ways that allow you to keep the types and/or property accessors involved in (de)serialization non-public, if you so desire (whether this is recommendable or not is an entirely different discussion, though...)

If you want to have non-public properties participating in (de)serialization with Json.NET, you can decorate those properties with Json.NET's own `[JsonProperty]` attribute. Or, alternatively, you might decorate the data model type(s) with the `[DataContract]` attribute, and all serializable properties (public or not) with the `[DataMember]` attribute.

comments.body:
A note on the rationale behind this: ASP.NET Core currently has a work-around for serializers not supporting `IAsyncEnumerable<T>`, and its work-around is to buffer the entire enumeration in-memory before passing it to the serializer as a `List<T>` instead. Apart from being inefficient, this work-around also has a problem if you create a stream that has no logical end, which is something I bumped into; I made an ASP.NET Core endpoint that streams status updates for as long as the client chooses to stay connected. Using `IAsyncEnumerable<T>`, it never sends any data, because ASP.NET Core thinks it can find the end of the sequence. I want to help ASP.NET Core get rid of this work-around, and in order to do that, at least the two core formatters it comes bundled with support for are going to need to support `IAsyncEnumerable<T>`.

I have an API proposal to this effect in for System.Text.Json, just waiting to hear back on that, and I have proofed my proposal with a working implementation.

Newtonsoft.Json is the other standard JSON formatter supported by ASP.NET Core.

I have searched for other NuGet packages where someone other than the original developer has contributed a package to the ecosystem sharing the same base name. It is not super common, but there definitely seems to be precedent. Would anybody get upset if I published a `Newtonsoft.Json.AsyncEnumerable` package with a description explaining clearly that it was developed and maintained independently?

@JamesNK If I could draw your attention to this issue specifically -- if I get no response I will eventually come to the understanding that it is just fine to publish my `Newtonsoft.Json.AsyncEnumerable` and will proceed to do so. I just want to make sure that if for whatever reason you don't think I should do this, you have had the opportunity to let me know. :-)

https://github.com/logiclrd/Newtonsoft.Json.AsyncEnumerable
You're welcome to publish your own package. You'll need to choose a different name though, as only official packages can start with "Newtonsoft" prefix.

I feel that this would best serve the community by being as discoverable as possible. Is there any possibility of getting my package accepted into the main Newtonsoft.Json codebase, as a contribution rather than a stand-alone project, and published alongside other Newtonsoft.Json packages?

Further background information: I have decided I want to try to submit contributions to get ASP.NET Core to a point where it no longer automatically buffers all outbound `IAsyncEnumerable` values it sees. The reason it buffers them is that the JSON converters don't support it. ASP.NET Core natively uses `System.Text.Json` but can have `Newtonsoft.Json` plugged into it as well. I am independently looking into `System.Text.Json` changes to support `IAsyncEnumerable` natively. It seems to be that it is basically impossible to make `Newtonsoft.Json` _directly_ support `IAsyncEnumerable` because of the wide range of older framework versions it explicitly targets. Based on that, my proposal is to provide a converter that can be easily added to `Newtonsoft.Json`'s serializer settings during initialization. But, I have a feeling that ASP.NET Core isn't going to consider it a solved problem if there is a completely independent third-party library providing the solution.
The Newtonsoft.Json serialize is synchronous. Sync over async leads to a number of problems. I don't want to make it an official feature.

Then I fear ASP.NET Core will never properly support `IAsyncEnumerable`. :-( I'll have to think about whether there might be some architecture to make it discoverable whether a formatter properly supports `IAsyncEnumerable`.

I just Googled this, and found a site outlining the following scenario:

- The thread pool has a limited number of threads. On my system this limit is not tiny (4K for my memory/architecture) but it is nevertheless quite finite.
- With sync over async, the thread initiating the operation might itself be a thread pool thread. Each new operation that comes in pulls a thread from the pool.
- It invokes the async operation, which sets up an underlying I/O and then returns. When that I/O is completed, it queues up a thread pool action to process it.
- While the async operation is running, the sync part at the top has to wait for it, which means blocking that thread pool thread it is occupying.
- If you manage to get as many overlapping I/O operations as there are thread pool threads, then the entire thread pool will be occupied by those sync top ends blocking on the completion of the underlying I/O operations. When those I/O operations complete, their continuations won't ever get scheduled because there are no free threads.

Thus, a deadlock arises.

So, my converter is only a band-aid -- it works in constrained testing scenarios, but wouldn't be a reliable scenario in a service scenario.

The contract for GetHashCode() does not guarantee the behavior you expect (unique values for unequal objects). It only guarantees that equal objects have equal HashCodes. (See https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.object.gethashcode?view=netcore-3.1#remarks for some cautions)

In fact, it could never guarantee that, by the pigeonhole principle. For example, in an object composed of two int values, there are 2^64 different configurations of that object yet only 2^32 possible outputs for GetHashCode(). There will necessarily be overlap.

Perhaps Dictionary<JValue, T>is not an appropriate container for whatever it is you're trying to do.

> ### Expected behavior
> GetHashCode() method of JValue object must return Unique HashCode for each elements returned from JObject.SelectTokens method.
> 
> ### Actual behavior
> For some object it returned same HashCode. Due to this if you try to add JValue objects into Dictionary you will get error like below because internally it uses HashCode as Key in Dictionary<object, xxx> instance.

comments.body: Dictionaries are by definition arbitrarily ordered - a special case like this makes no sense to bake into a general library

> [Dictionary keys] are by definition arbitrarily ordered

Agreed. So are POCO properties. Yet it makes lots of sense that custom ordering of the latter is allowed via `JsonPropertyAttribute.Order` and (e.g. within a custom contract resolver) `JsonProperty.Order`.

> a special case like this makes no sense to bake into a general library

Elaboration on this point would be appreciated.

It's not a thing in the json spec.

Json.Net is a library thats ~10 years old. You have a workaround for your special case. It's pretty difficult to justify adding this case to library thats this mature and has survived this long without the special casing at this point.

But: once again: if a low level json writer was arbitrarily reordering items, that would be a problem. This is a Dictionary - I'd be very shocked and surprised that there's a way to order them.

TL;DR This is a ["starts with -100 points" issue](https://blogs.msdn.microsoft.com/ericgu/2004/01/12/minus-100-points/)

> TL;DR This is a "starts with -100 points" issue

The implication being that some issues do not start with -100 points. Contrast this with what you linked:

> So, we decided on the additive approach instead, and worked hard to keep the complexity down. One way to do that is through the concept of “minus 100 points”. **Every feature starts out in the hole by 100 points**, which means that it has to have a significant net positive effect on the overall package.

So again, I think we agree. This feature, like all features, starts with -100 points.

> It's not a thing in the json spec.

Correct, I think. Not sure how this is relevant, though, since JSON.net allows custom ordering of JSON object keys when the keys come from .NET object properties.

> Json.Net is a library thats ~10 years old. You have a workaround for your special case. It's pretty difficult to justify adding this case to library thats this mature and has survived this long without the special casing at this point.

Again, mostly correct. It is about 14 years old. I have a partial workaround. The feature is indeed probably difficult to justify.

> if a low level json writer was arbitrarily reordering items, that would be a problem.

So... it's a problem that the current API allows customization of JSON object key ordering for .NET object properties. I disagree here, but it's a perfectly valid opinion for you to hold.

> This is a Dictionary - I'd be very shocked and surprised that there's a way to order them.

I'm sincerely trying to stand in your shoes on this, but I don't understand your "shock & surprise" here:

- Things with comparers can be ordered.
- Strings have comparers.
- JSON object keys are strings.
- JSON.net provides custom ordering when those keys are sourced from .NET object properties.
- JSON.net does not provide custom ordering when those keys are sourced from .NET dictionary types.

To be clear, I make no claim that this feature is easy to (a) implement or (b) integrate without breaking changes. I hope that it is both of those things, but if wishes were horses, beggars would ride.

---

I'm removing the "please" from the issue title, but not because I'm not a beggar. I am a beggar, as is almost any FOSS user making any request of the FOSS project they're using. I think the "please" implies I'm unwilling to take this on myself. I am willing. If I manage to schedule some time for it, I'll mention it here, just as a heads-up for other potential implementors/collaborators.

I was being a devil's advocate - I won't be implementing the feature. I like software I use to be and stay simple. I also like maintainers not to have to ask devils advocate questions that others could ask. I consider that a public service.

I don't think your feature is completely crazy but
a) _all_ features start with -100 
b) Dictionaries, no matter how comparable their keys or vaales *are not ordered* 
c) this is not a systemic issue affecting lots of cases - its a non-idiomatic JSON thing that you have a workaround for

I'm not suggesting you're crazy or this is unimplementable, but having a general library support a very specific rendering like this smells funny to me.

That's all, no harm intended.

- (a) Agreed, as mentioned above.
- (b) Agreed, but irrelevant as discussed above.
- (c) Agreed, but the workaround is partial, as mentioned above.

No offense taken. I think it's great you engaged with this. At the very least, our discussion has been a "smoke test" of the feature's reasonableness. Thanks.

In comparison, in the .Net framework it is both marked as `[Serializable]` and implements `ISerializable` and thus can be round-tripped successfully by Json.NET there.

comments.body: Applying a naming strategy to a type doesn't automatically make all its child objects also use that strategy. In this case `ExtraThings` is a child object.

That's fine and all, but then that probably means that `[JsonProperty]` shouldn't allow specifying `NamingStrategyParameters` if they aren't actually going to be used. This is misleading:

```csharp
public class Foo
{
    [JsonProperty(
      NamingStrategyType = typeof(CamelCaseNamingStrategy), // <-- this will be used
      NamingStrategyParameters = new object[] { true, true })] // <-- but these won't
    public IDictionary<string, int> Bar { get; set; }
}
```

In that example, the first of those `NamingStrategyParameters` is specifically related to the handling of dictionary keys, and it's applied to a dictionary, and yet they aren't used. That doesn't really follow the Principle of Least Surprise.

I've added a PR which allows those parameters to be bound to the property so that they will be used during serialization.

You _could_ implement your own `class MyDictionary : IDictionary<string, int>` and decorate it with `[JsonDictionary]` to control this behaviour, but then that means you're using different types to influence serialisation settings whereas typically you use `[JsonProperty]` to influence those regardless of type.

> That's fine and all, but then that probably means that [JsonProperty] shouldn't allow specifying NamingStrategyParameters if they aren't actually going to be used.

That is the naming strategy applied to that individual property. Yes those parameters will be used. The flag to say it should apply to dictionary keys however doesn't make sense in that context.

> You could implement your own class MyDictionary : IDictionary<string, int> and decorate it with [JsonDictionary] to control this behaviour, but then that means you're using different types to influence serialisation settings whereas typically you use [JsonProperty] to influence those regardless of type.

Yes I think the real problem is not that `[JsonProperty]` isn't working correctly, but that there seems to be no way to decorate a specific property of type `IDictionary<Key,Value>` or any other `Dictionary` for that matter, with a `namingStrategy` for it's keys.

Because I agree creating new dictionary just so you can set it's Json serialization options is something I'd rather avoid.
In my use case I'm trying to create a library where people can give an object which contains a dictionary of values. What I don't want to do is constrain them to use "JsonFixedDictionary" as a type.

A proposed solution could be that we could also use the `JsonDictionaryAttribute` on properties so we have control over how that property renders it's keys.
Any news on this? I just spend an hour pulling my hair out, posting on SO before I found this issue that explains it all.

comments.body:
I think you can do this yourself with a [custom contract resolver](https://www.newtonsoft.com/json/help/html/contractresolver.htm#CustomIContractResolverExamples).  See:

 1. [Json.NET require all properties on deserialization](https://stackoverflow.com/q/29655502/3744182).   

    This shows how to use a custom contract resolver to require all members be present during deserialization.  An exception is thrown if a member is not set during deserialization.

 2. [Json.NET make property required based on property type](https://stackoverflow.com/q/48327799/3744182).

    This is similar to the above except that no exception is thrown for unset optional members.

Demo of the second contract resolver here: https://dotnetfiddle.net/dFE5kd.

Thanks for your message, but I guess an easier way to do it is using the setting `MissingMemberHandling = MissingMemberHandling.Error;` (see https://stackoverflow.com/a/21032130/544947 ).

Although I think that defaults matter, so Newtonsoft.Json should detect if the target type is a Record (not possible to code in C# I guess), and if it is, default to `MissingMemberHandling.Error` to avoid NREs.

@knocte - `MissingMemberHandling = MissingMemberHandling.Error` solves a complimentary problem:

 1. If your **JSON** has a property that your **model** does not, and you want that to be an error, use `MissingMemberHandling = MissingMemberHandling.Error`.  

    This setting is useful when you want to check whether your data model binds to all the properties present in the incoming JSON.

    See: [MissingMemberHandling setting](https://www.newtonsoft.com/json/help/html/DeserializeMissingMemberHandling.htm).

 2. If your **model** has a property that your **JSON** does not,  and you want that to be an error, use `[JsonProperty(Required = Required.Always)]`.

    This attribute is useful when you want to enforce that the JSON contains some critical, non-optional property value.

    The two contract resolvers linked to [above](https://github.com/JamesNK/Newtonsoft.Json/issues/2116#issuecomment-517984069) automate the process of applying `Required = Required.Always` by applying it to all properties that are not optional, and do not have their own explicit setting already applied.

    See: [JsonPropertyAttribute required](https://www.newtonsoft.com/json/help/html/JsonPropertyRequired.htm).

Since you want an error when a value is *unset* (which leaves the property value null), I believe you fall into case 2, in which the JSON is missing a property.

Point of clarification: the code examples in the first message are describing _records_ not _discriminated unions_.  

I have this problem as well, and I believe it's emblematic of problems with F# records and serialization:

* the current algorithm creates an 'empty' instance of the type, which for F# may not be valid.  I'd argue that f# records do not have a valid 'empty' state.
* The proper algorithm would be to use the `FSharpType` and `FSharpValue` module functions to do something like the following:
  * determine if the destination type is a record via `FSharpType.IsRecordType`. if no, continue on current serialization strategy. if yes, 
  * get field information for the record and iterate through them, deserializing each property from the current json payload to get the final array of record fields
  * use `FSharpValue.MakeRecord` with the appropriate type and field arguments to create a fully-hydrated and correct record with no missing fields.

Over the process of making the field value array, optionality should be taken into account. IE if destination type is `'a option` and the key is not present, set `None` for that value. Any other missing value should be interpreted as a serialization failure, because F# records are more strict than C# classes.

> records not discriminated unions.

comments.body:
This appears to be by design.  Your type `EncryptedPropertyViaConstructor` has a single parameterized constructor.  In such a situation, JSON properties are matched to arguments of the constructor by name (modulo case), deserialized to the type of the matched argument, and then passed into the constructor as explained [here](https://stackoverflow.com/a/23017892).  There is no way for `IValueProvider.SetValue` to be called before the instance of your type is constructed, since `SetValue` encapsulates an *instance method* on an already-constructed instance.  And there would appear to be no need to do so afterwards, as Json.NET makes the (reasonable) assumption that passing a property value into the constructor is sufficient to set the property's value.

Your problem seems similar to the recent Stack Overflow question *[How to customize value setting during deserialization with contract resolver and value provider](https://stackoverflow.com/q/57030272/3744182)*; the answer [here](https://stackoverflow.com/a/57033833/3744182) offers some additional explanation and some workarounds.

Json.NET's implementation of self-referencing loop detection depends on the `object.Equals()` implementations of the underlying objects.  For details see:

 - [Why doesn't reference loop detection use reference equality?](https://stackoverflow.com/a/46938352/3744182).
 - [Issue  #401: Object reference equality should be used when checking for circular references](https://github.com/JamesNK/Newtonsoft.Json/issues/401#issuecomment-77711185)

If the implementations of `object.Equals()` for mocked objects differ between .Net Core 2.2 and 
.NET Framework 4.72, you'll get different results for reference loop detection.  

Using your own equality comparer on both frameworks, e.g. `ObjectReferenceEqualityComparer<object>` from [`IEqualityComparer<T>` that uses ReferenceEquals](https://stackoverflow.com/q/1890058/3744182), may make the two frameworks behave consistently.

Also, did you see [How to mock (with Moq) an interface that is serialized by Newtonsoft.json?](https://stackoverflow.com/q/55966212/3744182)?  The error looks to be identical.

This is intended behavior.  From https://www.newtonsoft.com/json/help/html/SerializationGuide.htm#Objects

 > By default a type's properties are serialized in opt-out mode. What that means is that **all public fields and properties with getters** are automatically serialized to JSON, and fields and properties that shouldn't be serialized are opted-out by placing JsonIgnoreAttribute on them. To serialize private members, the JsonPropertyAttribute can be placed on private fields and properties.

There is no documented restriction that the members must also have setters.

If you want to only serialize read/write members, you can do so with a custom contract resolver.  See e.g. [Is there a way to ignore get-only properties in Json.NET without using JsonIgnore attributes?](https://stackoverflow.com/q/18543482/3744182).

`True` is not a valid JSON token, according to https://json.org/.  Upload it to e.g. https://jsonlint.com/ or https://jsonformatter.curiousconcept.com/ and you will get an error.  This is also spelled out in [RFC 8259](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc8259) which [states](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc8259#section-3):

> ```
> 3.  Values
> 
>    A JSON value MUST be an object, array, number, or string, or one of
>    the following three literal names:
> 
>       false
>       null
>       true
> 
>    The literal names MUST be lowercase.  No other literal names are
>    allowed.
> 
>       value = false / null / true / object / array / number / string
> 
>       false = %x66.61.6c.73.65   ; false
> 
>       null  = %x6e.75.6c.6c      ; null
> 
>       true  = %x74.72.75.65      ; true
> 
> ```

Thus if Json.NET were to parse `True` as a `bool` then that would be an extension to the standard.  It already implements several such extensions (see [this issue](https://github.com/JamesNK/Newtonsoft.Json/issues/646) for a discussion) but apparently no such extension for `bool` parsing has been implemented.

You probably could, however, implement this as a custom `JsonConverter`.  For a few examples of such see:

 - [how to get newtonsoft to deserialize yes and no to boolean](https://stackoverflow.com/a/29892927/3744182)

 - [Convert an int to bool with Json.Net](https://stackoverflow.com/q/14427596/3744182)

 - [How to deserialize dodgy JSON (with improperly quoted strings, and missing brackets)?](https://stackoverflow.com/q/46788778/3744182).

You could [ask on stack overflow](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/tagged/json.net) if it isn't clear from the above how to write the converter.

`True` isn't valid JSON so the JsonTextReader would throw an exception when reading it.

If you have a string value, e.g. `"True"`, then you could write a JsonConverter as mentioned previously.

It should be noted that, in the following code, you are **not** actually reading directly from a stream:

>     Dim RDR As New System.IO.StreamReader(OFD.FileName)
>     Dim Json = New Newtonsoft.Json.JsonTextReader(RDR)
>     JRoot = JsonConvert.DeserializeObject(RDR.ReadToEnd)

What you are actually doing here is opening a `StreamReader`, allocating a `JsonTextReader`, then ignoring the `JsonTextReader` and reading the entire stream into a `string`, then parsing the `string`.  This violates the suggestion from [Performance Tips: Optimize Memory Use](https://www.newtonsoft.com/json/help/html/performance.htm) to deserialize large files directly from a stream.  

To deserialize directly from a stream in VB.NET, you would create a method like:

    Public Module JsonExtensions
        Public Function LoadFromFile(Of T)(path As String, Optional ByVal settings as JsonSerializerSettings = Nothing) As T
            Using reader As New System.IO.StreamReader(path)
                Using jsonReader as New Newtonsoft.Json.JsonTextReader(reader)
	                Return JsonSerializer.CreateDefault(settings).Deserialize(Of T)(jsonReader)
                End Using
            End Using
        End Function
    End Module

And then use it like:

	Dim JRoot as JToken = JsonExtensions.LoadFromFile(Of JToken)(OFD.FileName)

The fact that you're not actually streaming may account for some of your problem.

Perhaps instead of a secondary field/property, store the original strings in some dictionary (with your custom JsonConverter populating this dictionary during deserialization)? Or, if the order of the json properties from the original json object has to be maintained as well, just store the complete original json fragment representing the deserialized object in a (private) string variable?

That said, discussions like these are usually open-ended, as the definition of "_better way of doing this_" depends very much on your use case, your requirements and other constraints, and thus the only person to know what really is a "_better way_" is you.

Stumbling on this issue porting my projects from NetFramework to Net5.

I'm surprised this is not a more high profile issue since this is probably happening to many people since the existence of NetCore. Any project using json serialization for messages between micro-services using different framework will encounter this on basic primitive types. #1378 offers a workaround, but it's not perfect, and also requires old NetFramework services to be updated to support the inverse (netcore to netframework).

Since the issue haven't moved since 2019, should I assume it's not in the plan to offer a transparent fix officially?
This repo is (almost) dead. Use `System.Text.Json` instead. It makes no sense for MS to improve this serializer.

As much as `System.Text.Json` is a nice initiative and faster and easier to use for basic projects, it is still missing many features so the switch can't be done "as is" for many project. Notably polymorphic deserialization (TypeNameHandling) as mentioned in this issue. Or PopulateObject(), or some other custom converters that needs to be implemented differently.

Yes, there is no parity in features yet. But at least with the appearance of net5 there are more green checkmarks in the second column - https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/serialization/system-text-json-migrate-from-newtonsoft-how-to?pivots=dotnet-5-0#table-of-differences-between-newtonsoftjson-and-systemtextjson

comments.body:
It seems like this bug only happens when the child element with the identical name has no siblings.

For example, if your input XML is:
```
<location json:Array="true">
    <location>
        <name>Name of location.location 1</name>
    </location>
    <status>active</status>
</location>
```

Then JsonConvert.SerializeXmlNode will correctly convert it to:
```
"location": [
    {
        "location": {
            "name": "Name of location.location 1"
        },
        "status": "completed"
    }
]
```

Just adding that this fault is still happening in 13.01 when the child has the same name and is the only child.

Since this was reported 2 years ago, I guessed there wasn't a fix coming soon!
So here is what I did, maybe it helps others.

1) Step through the XML document and rename every node ( that could cause an issue)  to a unique name ( Name__1 , Name__2) , storing how many were renamed.
2) perform the SerializeXmlNode and get the correct json string. 
3) Replace all the occurrences of "Name__X" back to "Name" in the Json string

A bit cumbersome, but it works :)

Rob

I have the same issue.

Any news ?

After checking, actually double.MaxValue is 1.7976931348623157E+308
So 1.79769313486232E+308 is not a valid double.

Issue is in the external system.

For those who stumble upon this, an explanation of why this is the way it is:

1.79769313486232E+308 is a common 15-digit rounding of the 17-digit Max Value of a Double, 1.7976931348623157E+308.

Why is this a common problem?

By default, `double.ToString()` returns 15 digits of precision. Because of this, `double.MaxValue.ToString()` results in a return string of `"1.79769313486232E+308"`. This is not a valid double, but it is the 15-digit rounded version of double.MaxValue. You **must specify** that you want a round trip capable result if you want a truly safe string representation of a double. You do this with the "R" format string: `double.MaxValue.ToString("R")`. It is very odd, but here's the result of two lines of round trip parsing:

`double.Parse(double.MaxValue.ToString()) // Throws an exception`
`double.Parse(double.MaxValue.ToString("R")) // Executes fine and returns double.MaxValue`

So the short answer...the value you're using isn't a valid double. It's up to you to manually account for those edge cases or prevent them from forming by preemptively using the "R" format string on floating point values.

comments.body:
The default float parse handling is `FloatParseHandling.Double` thus when you deserialize to `JObject` it deserializes the value to a `double` and then when you call the generic `Value` method it then tries to convert the `double` to a `decimal`. When parsing to the `double` it must have rounded up due to floating point precision errors and then is no longer able to fit that value within a `decimal`. You can replicate this with the following line of code.

```c#
Convert.ToDecimal(double.Parse(decimal.MaxValue.ToString()));
```

The fix then is to use a `FloatParseHandling.Decimal` on the `JsonTextReader`.

If you can guarantee all the `double` values you're going to parse can be represented in a `decimal` value then just go with `FloatParseHandling.Decimal`. Otherwise you'll probably have to resort to creating C# classes to deserialize to with various `decimal` or `double` properties as opposed to deserializing to a `JObject`.

@TylerBrinkley's suggestion is the best one.

Or you could read the JSON manually with a JsonTextReader.

turns out, the Path property is not even correct to do this kind of things, so I'm afraid I don't think what I need can be done properly using Newtonsoft.Json. We ended up just rewrting most of the logic.

> turns out, the Path property is not even correct to do this kind of things, so I'm afraid I don't think what I need can be done properly using Newtonsoft.Json. We ended up just rewrting most of the logic.

I [asked a question on Stack Overflow](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/30304128/how-to-perform-partial-object-serialization-providing-paths-using-newtonsoft-j) on how to perform partial object serialization in order to reduce the footprint the JSON object some time ago.  User 'dbc' provided an excellent solution.

The scenario for my use case was that I was providing a really basic markup language to users that wanted to create custom data entry forms for our HTML application.  The markup would generate the HTML with data bindings and the corresponding JSON object which would become the binding context.

We provided a really rich object model that is too heavy for thin clients and the end-users would not care about much of the data in the model for their specific customizations.  In the markup, they would supply the "path" to the property to which they were binding (it handled single items as well as arrays) and the server, when processing the markup, would only return the JSON with the properties defined on the form.

This worked extremely well and the partial deserialization just worked as the user made updates.  We did have to handle some special cases (like users adding new items to collections), but overall, we achieved the end solution.

Note that the solution isn't the most ideal as it relies on serializing the entire object and then culling out only the items based on the paths the user provides.  However, the caller provides all the paths to the properties they want to keep and it does the rest.  Maybe this will help you with what you are trying to accomplish.

`MetadataPropertyHandling.Ignore` doesn't prevent the properties from being read, it prevents them from being read as metadata properties.

Use [JsonIgnore] to ignore if you don't want a property serialized.

This is during deserialization, and as described in the original bug I'm deserializing an `IDictionary<string, Valuetype>`, so I don't see how your suggestion would even work since dictionaries deserialization is special-cased - each element within JSON is deserialized as the `ValueType`.

I realize that `MetadataPropertyHandling` doesn't do this, which is why I thought a different property could be used to get the deserializer to skip over metadata properties automatically. The alternative is that we have to implement `JsonConverter.ReadJson` to handle this case ourselves when putting a `$schema` or `$comment` property in JSON is a common scenario that should be supported out of the box.

This is the scenario that JsonConverters are designed for: customizing how JSON is deserialized.

This is the first time this has ever been asked for so it isn't common.

Given Json.NET is the most popular JSON deserializer I figured handling this automatically (optionally, in a non-breaking way) would be a boon to developers, thus not requiring anyone deserializing a dictionary to handle this. Currently, even overriding `ReadJson` for a value type is non-optimal because the key property has already been read and there appears there's no way to swallow it, meaning the dictionary will have to contain the $schema and some dummy value that would later have to be ignored or removed. It would otherwise be very easy and more efficient to ignore this around where `CheckPropertyName` is called.

So you would not accept a pull request to handle this?

Every setting makes JsonSerializer bigger, and it is already very big.

I'd be ok with that property on JsonDictionaryContract. It could then be set in custom contract resolvers.

comments.body:
I have been thinking about this for a while now and I'm beginning to think that both of these properties should have a corresponding `$type` and `$values` in the serialized JSON.

The [documentation](https://www.newtonsoft.com/json/help/html/T_Newtonsoft_Json_TypeNameHandling.htm) states the following for `TypeNameHandling.Auto`:
> Include the .NET type name when the type of the object being serialized is not the same as its declared type. Note that this doesn't include the root serialized object by default. To include the root object's type name in JSON you must specify a root type object with SerializeObject(Object, Type, JsonSerializerSettings) or Serialize(JsonWriter, Object, Type).

If the library adheres to that description then it means that:
```csharp
(typeof(IList<string>) == typeof(List<string>)) == false
```

and that:
```csharp
(typeof(IList<string>) == (new [] { "a", "b", "c"}).GetType()) == false
```

Thus both of them should have their corresponding types written down. Actually, if the declaring type is an _interface_ or a _generic interface_, it should always output the `$type` property to know what implementation should be chosen once deserialization starts (unless null).

I'm not sure why it's not like that, so I'll let others chime in as I just started out with reading the source of Newtonsoft.Json :)

The type name isn't included with `IList<string>` and `List<string>` because Json.NET defaults to creating a `List<T>` for `IList<T>`, hence it is not needed.

If you always want it then use a setting other than auto.

comments.body:
Writing a `JsonReader` and `JsonWriter` that use `IBufferWriter<byte>` (and whatever the read equivalent is) would certainly be possible. Making the entire serializer async would be a huge amount of work and require a lot of duplication of code to have sync and async paths. I wouldn't really want to maintain that.

I'm not planning to work with pipelines myself right now, I have other things I want to add to the next version first, but a JsonReader and JsonWriter that used them directly would be useful and could live in an independent package.

How would you feel about a PR that makes your serialization code async (returning `ValueTask` for better perf) where it hardly ever actually yields, but may occasionally when the buffers need to wait for I/O? I don't anticipate that you'd have code duplication since the sync and async code paths would be implemented with the same methods.

As you might know this is currently a big issue when using asp.net core 3+.

I want my controllers to stream the data to the client instead of buffering it all, but asp.net core disallows synchronist streaming.
(read here https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/8302)

I bet the pullrequest AArnott mentioned didn't arive, but i find this a good direction, since the whole .net world is moving more and more towards async. Not supporting it is kinda biting yourself in the butt

@BasieP ASP.NET Core already evangelizes the System.Text.Json serializer. Is there some reason you can't just use that one in the new scenarios? 
Another option, that I actually use in StreamJsonRpc with Newtonsoft.Json, is buffer up the incoming data with my [`Sequence<T>` class](https://github.com/AArnott/Nerdbank.Streams/blob/master/doc/Sequence.md), then turn that into a `ReadOnlySequence<byte>` and [my `AsStream` extension method](https://www.fuget.org/packages/Nerdbank.Streams/2.6.81/lib/netstandard2.0/Nerdbank.Streams.dll/Nerdbank.Streams/StreamExtensions) from the same library and have newtonsoft.json (synchronously) deserialize from that.
For serialization, I do roughly the same thing: have newtonsoft.json write to a Stream from another `AsStream` method that wraps `Sequence<byte>` (via its `IBufferWriter<byte>` interface), then I asynchronously write out the underlying buffer.

While this doesn't allow *truly* streaming read/write, it's efficient. And it does *not* require allocating arbitrarily large contiguous blocks of memory the way `MemoryStream` would.

comments.body:
IMHO the announcement linked above is somewhat misleading, so hopefully people here won't mind if I add a few details about the current state of spans in .NET.

It is important to know that using spans would be an optimization that's **currently only feasible on .NET Core ≥2.1** because, at this time, there is no other .NET platform that fully supports spans.

By "full support", I am referring to three separate requirements:

1. Availability of the base types `Span<T>`, `ReadOnlySpan<T>`, `Memory<T>`, and `ReadOnlyMemory<T>`.

2. Availability of APIs in the BCL that use the above types. (Without dedicated APIs, spans are about as useful as `System.ArraySegment<T>`—that is, not useful at all.)

3. Recognition of the above types by the .NET runtime's JIT compiler for efficient code generation. (Only with runtime support are spans really as "fast" as plain array index or pointer operations. Without runtime support, they might even cause additional overhead.)

Concerning the .NET Framework, you can get (1) via the NuGet package `System.Memory`. But you might be out of luck regarding (2) and (3) as the classic .NET Framework will likely never have BCL nor JIT support for spans—see https://github.com/Microsoft/dotnet/issues/770.

Concerning .NET Standard, BCL support for spans is ~~apparently~~ planned for ~~vNext—see https://github.com/dotnet/standard/issues/682#issuecomment-401947585~~ [.NET Standard 2.1](https://github.com/dotnet/standard/blob/fe8d520d5ab2d5cdf281222329ff83d96b09f7f4/docs/planning/netstandard-2.1/README.md).

This could be an indication that full span runtime support (3) might eventually make it into platforms other than .NET Core (most notably, Mono and Mono-based runtimes—see e.g. https://github.com/mono/mono/issues/7249).

I am also linking to https://github.com/Tornhoof/SpanJson for those who are interested in seeing spans at work in JSON parsing.

@stakx so (3) indirectly states you should not use aspnetcore 2.1 on .NET Framework although being a valid target. I have not noticed a warning so far that it will be slower than aspnetcore 2.0 when not used on netcore.

@springy76, let's not get too sidetracked here, but... that is interesting. I am not familiar with ASP.NET Core, but assuming that 2.1 makes heavy use of spans, I cannot say how they were able to get it working on top of the .NET Framework. Not so much because of the missing JIT support (3), which would just make it slower, but because of missing BCL APIs (2), which would make it impossible to compile and run.
Anything with span would wait until netstandard3.0 when the Span APIs are available.
Spans are now planned for inclusion in [.NET Standard 2.1](https://github.com/dotnet/standard/blob/master/docs/planning/netstandard-2.1/README.md).

This blog post (and a comment underneath) seems to imply that .NET Framework 4.8 will have the JIT improvements for `Span<T>` and similar - though the additional Span<T> APIs (which would then only be available via `System.Memory`), and only for 64-bit: https://blogs.msdn.microsoft.com/dotnet/2018/09/17/announcing-net-framework-4-8-early-access-build-3646/
>**Runtime – JIT improvements**

I think I may see your difficulty. There is no API `JToken.DeepEquals(string, string)`. Instead, there are the following two APIs: 1. [`JToken.DeepEquals(JToken t1, JToken t2)`](https://www.newtonsoft.com/json/help/html/M_Newtonsoft_Json_Linq_JToken_DeepEquals.htm) which compares two `JToken` objects, and 2. [`JTokenImplicit Conversion (String to JToken)`](https://www.newtonsoft.com/json/help/html/M_Newtonsoft_Json_Linq_JToken_op_Implicit_29.htm) which performs an implicit conversion from `String` to `JToken`.

As noted in the [docs](https://www.newtonsoft.com/json/help/html/M_Newtonsoft_Json_Linq_JToken_op_Implicit_29.htm) this method returns *the `JValue` initialized with the specified value.* I.e. the incoming string is converted to a JSON **string literal** rather than parsed into a JSON **object**. Thus your sample code is equivalent to the following: string s1 = JsonConvert.SerializeObject(o1); string s2 = JsonConvert.SerializeObject(o2); JToken token1 = s1; // Implicit conversion to JToken JToken token2 = s2; // Implicit conversion to JToken Console.WriteLine(JToken.DeepEquals(token1, token2)); Which results in `false` because the two strings `s1` and `s2` **interpreted as JSON string literals** are in fact distinct. This issue isn't limited to Json.NET, Microsoft's System.Text.Json does also raise an exception.

This is because DateTimeOffset values are converted to UTC internally, and when the value "0001-01-01T00:00:00" is deserialized to DateTimeOffset, it will use the local timezone. [https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.datetimeoffset.minvalue](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.datetimeoffset.minvalue?view=netcore-3.0):
> Any DateTimeOffset value is converted to Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) before the method performs the comparison with MinValue. This means that a DateTimeOffset value whose date and time are close to the minimum range, but whose offset is positive, may throw an exception. For example, the value 1/1/0001 1:00:00 AM +02:00 is out of range because it is one hour earlier than MinValue when it is converted to UTC.

> ### Explanation
> Decimals in .NET are tricky: besides the number itself, they store the number of digits necessary to represent it. > ### Steps to reproduce

> using Newtonsoft.Json;
> using System;
> 
> namespace JsonDecimalIssue
> {
>     class Program
>     {
>         static void Main(string[] args)
>         {
>             decimal before = 15;
>             string serialized = JsonConvert.SerializeObject(before); // produces "15.0" <- incorrect
>             decimal after = JsonConvert.DeserializeObject<decimal>(serialized);

>             Console.WriteLine(before); // Writes "15"
>             Console.WriteLine(after);  // Writes "15.0"
>             Console.ReadKey();
>         }
>     }
> }
> ```
> 
> ### Possible solution
> The issue can be solved by keeping the necessary number of decimal digits in JSON representation of the number, e.g. serialize decimal 15 as integer "15", and decimal 15.0 as "15.0".
